vignette:
Amina is twenty-five years old, a nurse, and she has been living with her boyfriend, Daniel, for the past year in a small apartment that smells of antiseptic and jasmine tea. She came to the United States as a refugee three years ago, after the fighting reached her hometown in a coastal African city. She does not like to talk about the war, but she can feel it pressing against her skin every day.

The event that most often comes back to her happened on a Tuesday morning, during a lull in the shelling. She had been a student nurse then, working at a small clinic near the port. A child had been brought in with shrapnel wounds—a boy, maybe seven years old, covered in dust and blood. Amina was holding his hand, trying to keep him still while the doctor worked. She remembers the boy’s eyes, huge and dark, fixed on her face. He was saying something, but the shelling had made her ears ring so badly she could not hear. She remembers nodding, squeezing his hand, telling him it would be okay. Then the second explosion hit. It was closer than any she had ever felt. The ceiling came down. When she opened her eyes, the boy was gone—not dead, just gone, buried under rubble. She never saw him again. She does not know if he survived.

Now, in the present, Amina works the night shift on a surgical ward. Her colleagues describe her as efficient, quiet, and always first to volunteer for the most critical cases. But what they do not see is how she plans escape routes every time she enters a patient’s room. She positions her body so that her back is never to the door. When a loud instrument tray clatters to the floor, her heart slams into her throat and she freezes for three full seconds, the sound of the falling ceiling echoing in her ears. She then forces a smile and says, “Just a little jumpy tonight.” She avoids triage on busy nights because the crying of a child in the waiting room makes her palms sweat and her chest tighten. She has asked to be reassigned to adult patients only, but she cannot explain why.

At home, Amina is on alert. She checks the locks on the door four times before she sits down to eat. She cannot sleep unless Daniel is beside her, but his presence does not soothe her the way it used to. She lies awake, listening for sirens that do not come, her muscles coiled. She has nightmares that do not replay the explosion exactly, but instead show her looking for the boy in endless piles of rubble, unable to find him. She wakes gasping, and Daniel reaches for her, but she pulls away. She feels numb during the day, detached from him, from herself. She used to love cooking—now she eats standing up, distracted, tasting nothing.

She avoids the news. She cannot watch anything about war, not even a fictional film. When a friend’s social media post shows a flag from her home country, she scrolls past so fast her thumb aches. She feels a constant, low-grade guilt, as if she abandoned something by surviving, by leaving. She has not told Daniel the full story. She told him about the bombing in general terms, but not about the boy, not about the feeling of his small hand slipping away. She is afraid that if she says it out loud, she will fall apart, and she needs to be strong. She is a nurse. She has to be.

The PCL-5 score of 45 reflects what Amina herself does not name: hyperarousal that makes her pace the hallway after a shift, intrusive memories that surface when she smells blood or bleach, emotional detachment that isolates her from Daniel, and a constant startle reflex that leaves her exhausted. She came to therapy because Daniel begged her—because she was weepy for no reason and then shut down completely. She sits in the chair now, her hands folded, her eyes scanning the room once before she looks at the therapist. She begins to speak, but she does not start with the bullet or the rubble. She starts with the boy’s eyes. She cannot remember his name, but she remembers the way his fingers curled around hers. And she says, very quietly, “I think he was still alive when I let go.”
